misconceptions.statement: Everyone is born with no immunity at all until they get a vaccine or disease.
misconceptions.why: Students link immunity only with vaccines and medicines they have seen.
misconceptions.fix: We are born with innate immunity such as skin, mucus and some white blood cells that act against all germs.

probe.question: Does a newborn baby have any defence against germs before any vaccine?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Skin is just a covering and plays no part in fighting germs.
misconceptions.why: Skin is seen as a body covering, not as part of a defence system.
misconceptions.fix: Skin, mucus, tears and stomach acid block or kill germs; they are the first line of defence.

probe.question: Which of these helps fight germs: skin, mucus, stomach acid?
probe.wrong_answer: None of them, only white blood cells fight germs

misconceptions.root_belief: a part has only its obvious everyday job

misconceptions.statement: If you have immunity to one disease you are protected against all diseases.
misconceptions.why: The word immunity is used generally as 'strong body'.
misconceptions.fix: Acquired immunity is specific: antibodies for measles do not protect against typhoid.

probe.question: A child had measles and is immune to it. Is the child protected from chickenpox?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, immunity protects against all diseases

misconceptions.statement: Antibodies are living cells that eat germs.
misconceptions.why: Students merge antibodies with white blood cells, which do engulf germs, and treat anything in the blood that fights germs as a living cell.
misconceptions.fix: Antibodies are protein molecules made by white blood cells. They bind to a specific antigen and mark or neutralise it. They are not living cells.

probe.question: Are antibodies living cells or proteins? Which do they do: eat germs, or stick to germs?
probe.wrong_answer: Antibodies are living cells that swallow germs.

misconceptions.root_belief: Defence molecules and defence cells are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A vaccine works by giving the body ready-made antibodies from outside.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse vaccination with antibody injections or antiserum, and think protection is handed over rather than built by the body.
misconceptions.fix: A vaccine contains an antigen (weakened, killed or part of a germ). The body's own white blood cells make antibodies and memory cells in response.

probe.question: After a vaccine, who makes the antibodies that protect you?
probe.wrong_answer: The vaccine itself contains the antibodies and passes them into the body.

misconceptions.root_belief: Protection is delivered ready-made, not built by the body
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about vaccination

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines protect the moment they are given.
misconceptions.why: Students think of a vaccine like a medicine that acts at once, and ignore the time the body needs to make antibodies and memory cells.
misconceptions.fix: The body takes days to weeks to build a response after vaccination. Protection is not full immediately, and some vaccines need several doses.

probe.question: A child gets a measles vaccine in the morning and is exposed to measles that evening. Is the child fully protected?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the vaccine protects at once.

misconceptions.statement: Herd immunity means every single person in the group has become immune.
misconceptions.why: The word 'herd' and 'immunity' suggest everyone is immune, so students miss that it works when most, not all, are immune.
misconceptions.fix: Herd immunity needs a large majority to be immune. This reduces spread so that the few who are not vaccinated are also protected.

probe.question: In a village 90% are vaccinated. Can herd immunity still protect the 10% who are not?
probe.wrong_answer: No, herd immunity works only if every person is immune.

misconceptions.root_belief: Group protection needs every member protected

misconceptions.statement: Herd immunity means that if I am vaccinated, I do not need others to be vaccinated.
misconceptions.why: Students think immunity is only a personal matter, so protection of the community does not depend on others' choices.
misconceptions.fix: Protection of the community depends on many people being vaccinated. If too many skip vaccines, disease spreads again and even some vaccinated and vulnerable people are at risk.

probe.question: If many people in a town refuse vaccines, does it affect a vaccinated person's safety?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a vaccinated person is completely safe whatever others do.

misconceptions.root_belief: Immunity is only an individual matter

misconceptions.statement: Vaccines under India's immunisation programme are given only when a child falls ill.
misconceptions.why: Students link giving a medicine with being sick, so they treat vaccines as treatment rather than scheduled prevention.
misconceptions.fix: The Universal Immunisation Programme gives free vaccines like BCG, polio and measles to healthy children on a schedule, before they get the disease.

probe.question: When is a healthy baby given BCG and polio drops under the immunisation programme?
probe.wrong_answer: Only after the baby has fallen ill with TB or polio.

misconceptions.root_belief: Vaccines are a treatment for existing illness

misconceptions.statement: Antibiotics are painkillers or fever medicines that make any illness better.
misconceptions.why: Antibiotics are commonly prescribed together with other medicines, so students think they treat symptoms and all illnesses.
misconceptions.fix: Antibiotics act only on bacteria, by killing them or stopping their growth. They do not reduce pain or fever directly and do not work on viruses.

probe.question: A child has a viral fever. Will an antibiotic cure it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, antibiotics work on every fever and illness.

misconceptions.source_hint: studies on public understanding of antibiotics

misconceptions.statement: When antibiotics are overused, the person's body gets used to the medicine and stops responding.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the idea of habit or tolerance seen with other substances to the person rather than to the bacteria.
misconceptions.fix: Bacteria become resistant when the survivors of antibiotic use multiply. The person's body does not become resistant.

probe.question: After many antibiotic courses, what has become resistant: the person or the bacteria?
probe.wrong_answer: The person's body gets used to the antibiotic and no longer responds.

misconceptions.root_belief: The patient's body adapts, not the germs

misconceptions.statement: It is fine to stop antibiotics as soon as you feel better.
misconceptions.why: Students judge a medicine by symptoms, so feeling well seems to mean all the bacteria are gone.
misconceptions.fix: Feeling better does not mean all bacteria are dead. Stopping early leaves some alive, and the survivors may be resistant. The full course should be finished.

probe.question: After two days of a five-day antibiotic course the patient feels fine. Should the patient stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, once the symptoms are gone the medicine is no longer needed.

misconceptions.root_belief: No symptoms means the germs are gone
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on public understanding of antibiotics
